name: Neck stretches / chin tucks
lead: A chin tuck is a small retraction movement in which the chin is drawn straight back, without nodding the head down, so the head sits over the shoulders and the deep neck flexors work. Neck stretches are often paired with it to loosen the back of the neck. Both come from physical therapy for posture-related neck complaints, and in looksmaxxing forums they are used to improve how the head and neck look in profile: a head that sits further back over the spine changes how the chin, jaw and neck line up in photos and in person. [1][2][3]

On looksmax.org, proponents say regular chin tucks, sometimes weighted and often combined with weighted neck curls, improve neck posture and, in their view, raise the hyoid area so the soft region under the chin looks tighter. Some posters share before-and-after photos. [3][4][8]

Clinical sources describe strengthening the deep neck flexors, including longus colli, within the management of forward head posture and neck pain, and a 2024 randomised trial found that adding stabilisation exercises to a McKenzie programme reduced chronic neck pain more than McKenzie exercises alone. [1][5][6] No published study located for this article has examined chin tucks for hyoid position, jawline definition or facial appearance.
infobox: Deep neck flexors (e.g. longus colli); stretches target upper trapezius and suboccipital muscles [1][12]
Neck curls, wall or towel-weighted chin tucks [4]

paras: A chin tuck draws the chin back horizontally so the ears move over the shoulders, as opposed to nodding the chin down. It is practised lying down, against a wall or seated, and in forums is sometimes made harder with towels or weights placed to resist the movement. [4][18]

Neck stretches are the companion practice: gentle movements that lengthen the upper trapezius, suboccipital and other posterior neck muscles. One T Nation forum post describes a short daily routine of small head circles and tilting the head back to stretch the front of the neck. [21] Neck curls are the loaded form, in which the neck flexes against resistance, and are often discussed in the same breath. [3][22]

Wikipedia's forward head posture article lists strengthening of the deep neck flexors and neck retractors, and stretching of the upper trapezius, sternocleidomastoid, scalenes and suboccipital muscles, among commonly recommended measures, noting that some of those claims need independent confirmation. It does not name chin tucks specifically. [1] Wikipedia's neck pain article states that craniocervical flexion motor-control exercises are effective for non-specific chronic neck pain and that specific strengthening exercises may improve function and pain. [5]

Longus colli is a muscle on the front of the cervical spine, running from the atlas to the third thoracic vertebra, and its listed action is flexing the neck and head. [12] It is commonly injured in whiplash. [12]

The hyoid bone, which forums name as the target of neck work, is a horseshoe-shaped bone in the front midline of the neck between the chin and the thyroid cartilage. It has almost no direct bony joints and is held by muscles and ligaments, including suprahyoid muscles above it (such as the digastric and mylohyoid) and infrahyoid muscles below it (such as the sternohyoid and thyrohyoid). [11] It supports the tongue, larynx and swallowing, and a lower hyoid position is associated with obstructive sleep apnoea. [11] Wikipedia's hyoid article does not discuss its effect on the look of the area under the chin.

A 1983 plastic-surgery paper on platysma cords, the vertical bands that show in the front of the neck, attributed them to stretching of skin, fat and the superficial musculoaponeurotic system with age, and recommended tightening those tissues and supporting the muscle in a more youthful position. [14] It does not address exercise.

Forward head posture is described as a pattern in which the head sits ahead of the shoulders, linked with prolonged hunching over laptops and phones. In the pattern described on Wikipedia, the deep neck flexors weaken while the posterior neck muscles shorten and strain, so the chin pokes forward. Commonly cited visual signs are an earlobe that sits ahead of a vertical line through the shoulder bone and a protruding chin. [1]

Neck pain prevalence in adults aged 15 to 75 has ranged from about 5.9 to 22.2 percent in the studies cited there. A 2019 systematic review reported that forward head posture correlates with neck pain in adults but not in adolescents. [1] That page also says the evidence for specific exercise protocols is thin and several recommendations are flagged as needing confirmation. [1]

Posture retraction exercises have a clinical lineage in physiotherapy. Robin McKenzie, a New Zealand physiotherapist, developed the method that bears his name from the late 1950s and launched it in 1981 as Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy; its central idea is directional movement that moves symptoms toward the spine's midline. [13] Wikipedia notes that evidence reviews of the method, mostly in low back pain, show small to moderate effects and methodological limitations. [13]

The appearance use belongs to looksmaxxing, which Wikipedia says began in 2010s incel and manosphere forums and moved to TikTok in the early 2020s, where creators framed it as self-improvement. [15] Neck exercise threads on looksmax.org show a recurring cycle of 'cope or real' questions and progress posts. [3][4][19][20][22]

Posters describe chin tucks done against a wall or lying down, with towels or weights for resistance, and neck curls as a progression. [4][18] One poster described three sets of 20 repetitions. [3] Another thread asks for the most efficient way to perform chin tucks, and one titled 'proper neck curls' discusses form. [18]

Posters link neck work to several goals: raising the hyoid area, a tighter submental look, a wider jaw, a deeper voice and better posture. [3][8][16] Results are reported as photos and anecdotes. [4][8]

A 2024 randomised clinical trial in an outpatient physical therapy clinic assigned 76 patients with chronic non-specific neck pain to six weeks of McKenzie exercises alone (posture correction, range-of-motion work and lateral neck stretches) or McKenzie exercises plus cervical and scapulothoracic stabilisation training. The combined group had a greater reduction in current pain intensity, a mean difference of 1.2 points on a 0 to 10 scale, and neck disability improved in both groups. [6]

A 2020 study of 119 head and neck cancer survivors examined neck range of motion and twice-daily neck stretches alongside swallowing exercises over 12 weeks, a clinical setting unrelated to appearance. [7]

Gentle retraction exercises are discussed in the clinical sources above as part of conservative neck care. In forums, members report neck pain in some threads, one asking whether neck discomfort during chin tucks is normal, and another titled around feeling sick after neck curls. [10][17] Added load raises demand on the cervical spine, and posters who add weight describe improvising with towels. [4]

Wikipedia's longus colli article describes neck injury in whiplash and rare calcific tendinitis causing neck pain and difficulty swallowing; these are unrelated to exercise but show that neck pain with swallowing symptoms is a medical presentation. [12]

Forum threads ask whether chin tucks and neck curls are 'cope or real.' In one, a respondent said they are worthwhile unless the person expects them to transform overall attractiveness, and when the poster said they simply wanted to raise the hyoid, another said these are the best exercises for that area. The original poster described doing three sets of 20 repetitions. [3]

Another poster shared photos after adding weight to chin tucks, saying face fat and body weight were unchanged and that their posture was improving day by day, and described using stacked towels to add resistance. [4] A separate thread shows a before-and-after neck-curl progress post in which replies ask how long the poster had trained. [8] Other thread titles ask whether neck exercises can widen the jaw, whether chin tucks deepen the voice, and why neck discomfort appears during chin tucks. [9][10][16] These are anecdotes; no controlled data accompany them.

No studies found on chin tucks or neck stretches for facial or jawline appearance. Research on related exercises concerns neck pain and function rather than aesthetics, including the 2024 randomised trial of stabilisation exercises in chronic neck pain described above. [6][5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, chin tucks and neck curls are a recurring topic, often framed as a test of whether neck work produces visible change.[3][4][8]

claims.claim: Chin tucks and neck curls raise the hyoid area
claims.believers: Posters say these are the best exercises for improving the hyoid region and a tighter neck-to-chin look.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined hyoid position or submental appearance after chin tuck training; clinical literature addresses deep neck flexor strengthening for pain and posture.[5]

claims.claim: Adding weight to chin tucks makes visible before-and-after changes
claims.believers: One poster reported photos showing a difference at the same weight and facial fat after weighted chin tucks.[4]
claims.experts: No controlled studies are available; photo differences can reflect posture, angle and lighting, and none have been studied in this context.[1]

claims.claim: Chin tucks correct forward head posture
claims.believers: Forum users describe improved posture after daily practice.[4]
claims.experts: Clinical sources list deep neck flexor strengthening among approaches to forward head posture and chronic neck pain, with some statements flagged as needing confirmation; a 2024 trial found stabilisation exercises added to McKenzie exercises reduced chronic neck pain.[1][6][5]

claims.claim: Neck curls plus chin tucks give visible facial or neck change
claims.believers: Posters in neck-curl progress threads share photos as proof and ask how long others trained.[8]
claims.experts: No published study has examined facial appearance after neck-flexor training.

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title asserts or asks whether chin tucks make the voice deeper. [16]
claims.experts: No published study located examines chin tucks and voice pitch.

claims.believers: Posters ask whether chin tucks and neck curls help the jaw get wider. [9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's neck and neck-pain pages describe neck muscles in terms of function and pain, and no study located measures jaw width after neck exercise. [2][5]

card.summary: Deep neck flexor exercise used in physio for posture; forums claim it lifts the hyoid area, but no appearance studies exist.
card.aka: Chin tucks, neck curls, neck retraction
card.note: Posture and pain use has clinical support; appearance claims have not been studied.

quick.overview:
Chin tucks pull the chin straight back to engage the deep neck flexors, and weighted versions are called neck curls. Physical therapy sources use similar exercises for forward head posture and neck pain.

Looksmax.org users say they improve neck posture and raise the hyoid area. No studies have examined those appearance claims.
quick.mechanism: The movement retracts the head over the shoulders and activates deep flexors such as longus colli. Forum believers say stronger flexors change how the chin and neck meet; this mechanism for appearance has not been tested.
quick.risks: Gentle exercise is generally low risk, but users report neck pain in some threads, and added weight raises load on the cervical spine. People with existing neck conditions are typically advised by clinicians to get assessed first.

chain: Deep neck flexors are trained and neck muscles stretched
Head sits further back over the shoulders
Chin and neck line up better in profile and photos
angle.text: Chin tucks aim to pull a forward-set head back over the spine, which changes how the chin, jaw and neck line up when seen from the side. Practitioners use them, often with neck curls, in the hope of a cleaner neck-to-chin line and a tighter-looking submental area.
